questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: The SAFE Mortgage Licensing Act of 2008 established minimum standards for mortgage loan originator licensing and registration nationwide. The SAFE Act was enacted primarily to:

answers.text: Set maximum interest rates on all residential mortgage loans
Protect consumers and reduce fraud by establishing minimum standards for MLO licensing and registration through the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System
Replace RESPA and TILA with a single unified federal mortgage disclosure
Require all mortgage lenders to obtain federal bank charters

explanations.a: Wrong — the SAFE Act addresses licensing, not rate limits.
explanations.b: Correct — the SAFE Act's stated purpose is consumer protection through minimum licensing standards and the NMLS.
explanations.c: Wrong — RESPA and TILA disclosure rules are separate from the SAFE Act.
explanations.d: Wrong — the SAFE Act does not require federal bank charters.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: The SAFE Act establishes minimum pre-licensing education hours for state-licensed MLOs. Required content covers federal law, ethics, and non-traditional mortgage products. The minimum pre-licensing education requirement under the SAFE Act for a state-licensed MLO is:

answers.text: 20 hours, including at least 3 hours on federal law, 3 hours on ethics, and 2 hours on non-traditional mortgage lending
40 hours, including 20 hours of mandatory classroom instruction
10 hours with no specific content requirements
8 hours per year for each year of the license period

explanations.a: Correct — 12 USC 5105 requires 20 pre-licensing hours with specified content requirements.
explanations.b: Wrong — 40 hours is not the SAFE Act minimum.
explanations.c: Wrong — 10 hours with no content requirements does not meet the SAFE Act standard.
explanations.d: Wrong — 8 hours per year is the annual continuing education requirement, not pre-licensing.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Candidates for state MLO licensure must pass a written examination covering federal and state law. The SAFE Act sets a minimum passing standard. The minimum passing score on the SAFE Act National Test is:

answers.text: 100% correct (no errors permitted)
90% correct
75% correct
60% correct

explanations.a: Wrong — 100% is not the threshold; the SAFE Act permits some errors.
explanations.b: Wrong — 90% exceeds the minimum passing standard.
explanations.c: Correct — 12 USC 5107 establishes a 75% minimum passing score.
explanations.d: Wrong — 60% is below the SAFE Act minimum passing threshold.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Licensed MLOs must complete continuing education annually to maintain their license. The SAFE Act specifies mandatory content areas within the annual requirement. The minimum annual continuing education requirement under the SAFE Act is:

answers.text: 20 hours per year with no specific content requirements
6 hours per year with no content area mandates
12 hours per year covering federal and state law
8 hours per year, including 3 hours of federal law, 2 hours of ethics, 2 hours of non-traditional lending, and 1 hour of elective

explanations.a: Wrong — 20 hours is the pre-licensing requirement, not annual CE.
explanations.b: Wrong — 6 hours is below the SAFE Act CE minimum.
explanations.c: Wrong — 12 hours is not the SAFE Act annual CE standard.
explanations.d: Correct — 12 USC 5106 requires 8 annual CE hours with those content minimums.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: The NMLS assigns each licensed MLO a unique identifier that tracks licensing status and complaints. Consumers may verify an MLO's status using the identifier. The NMLS unique identifier must be:

answers.text: Disclosed only to the state regulator upon written request
Disclosed to consumers on loan applications, solicitation materials, and advertisements
Kept confidential to protect the MLO's professional privacy
Changed each time the MLO moves to a new employer

explanations.a: Wrong — the identifier is publicly disclosed, not restricted to regulators.
explanations.b: Correct — 12 USC 5104 and state rules require disclosure on applications and marketing materials.
explanations.c: Wrong — the identifier is public, not confidential.
explanations.d: Wrong — the identifier is permanent and does not change with each employer change.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: The SAFE Act creates two pathways: state licensure for most MLOs and federal registration for employees of federally regulated depositories. The pathway determines the regulatory framework. Employees of federally regulated depository institutions must:

answers.text: Register with the NMLS through their institution's Federal Registry rather than obtaining a state MLO license
Obtain both a state license and a federal registration simultaneously
Pass the same state licensing exam required of non-depository MLOs
Submit fingerprints only to their employer, not to the NMLS

explanations.a: Correct — depository-employee MLOs register through the NMLS Federal Registry under 12 USC 5113.
explanations.b: Wrong — federal registrants do not also hold state licenses.
explanations.c: Wrong — federal registrants are not required to pass the state exam under the SAFE Act.
explanations.d: Wrong — fingerprints are submitted to the NMLS/FBI background check system.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: State-licensed MLOs must pass an FBI background check. Certain criminal history disqualifies an applicant. An applicant for an MLO license may be denied on criminal-history grounds for:

answers.text: Any misdemeanor conviction in the past 10 years regardless of its nature
Any criminal offense, no matter how minor, appearing anywhere in their record
A DUI conviction occurring within 3 years of application
A felony involving fraud, dishonesty, breach of trust, or money laundering within the past 7 years, or any such felony involving financial crimes

explanations.a: Wrong — minor misdemeanors do not automatically disqualify; felonies of the specified type do.
explanations.b: Wrong — minor, unrelated offenses do not necessarily result in denial.
explanations.c: Wrong — a DUI alone is not the basis for mandatory disqualification under the SAFE Act.
explanations.d: Correct — 12 USC 5105 bars MLO licensure for those with such felonies within 7 years (or ever for financial crimes).

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: MLOs must keep their NMLS record current by reporting changes. Timely updates ensure the regulatory record is accurate. Material changes to an MLO's NMLS record, such as a change of employer, must generally be reported within:

answers.text: 90 days of the change
60 days of the change
30 days of the change
5 business days of the change

explanations.a: Wrong — 90 days exceeds most states' reporting deadlines.
explanations.b: Wrong — 60 days exceeds most states' reporting deadlines.
explanations.c: Correct — most states require NMLS updates within 30 days of a material change.
explanations.d: Wrong — 5 business days is shorter than most state requirements.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: An MLO with a personal financial interest in a settlement service provider must disclose that interest before making a referral. Undisclosed conflicts undermine the borrower's ability to choose freely. An MLO's duty to disclose conflicts of interest:

answers.text: Applies only when the conflict involves a title company or escrow firm
Requires the MLO to disclose any personal financial interest in a referred service provider to the borrower before or at the time of the referral
Is satisfied by a single boilerplate disclosure at consummation
Is optional when the referral fee is less than $500

explanations.a: Wrong — the disclosure duty applies to any settlement service provider.
explanations.b: Correct — RESPA and ethical standards require disclosure of financial interests before referrals.
explanations.c: Wrong — disclosure must occur at or before the referral, not only at consummation.
explanations.d: Wrong — there is no dollar-amount threshold that waives the disclosure duty.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Regulation Z's loan originator compensation rule prevents compensation from creating perverse incentives. The dual-compensation prohibition closes a loophole. Under the LO compensation rule, an MLO who receives consumer-paid compensation:

answers.text: May not also receive compensation from another person in the same transaction
May receive compensation from both the consumer and the lender if fully disclosed
May receive points from the consumer and a yield spread premium from the lender
May be paid by the settlement agent for processing services in the same transaction

explanations.a: Correct — 12 CFR 1026.36(d)(2) prohibits dual compensation in a single transaction.
explanations.b: Wrong — disclosure does not cure dual compensation; it is prohibited.
explanations.c: Wrong — yield spread premiums cannot be paid alongside consumer-paid comp under 1026.36.
explanations.d: Wrong — third-party settlement-agent compensation is also prohibited under the dual-comp rule.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Receiving undisclosed payments from settlement service providers in exchange for referrals is a RESPA violation. The prohibition eliminates backdoor compensation. An MLO who receives an undisclosed payment from a title company in exchange for referring borrowers to that company:

answers.text: Has committed a TRID violation only with no criminal exposure
Has committed an ethics violation but not a legal violation
Is in violation only if the borrower was charged more than the disclosed amount
Has violated RESPA Section 8's prohibition on kickbacks and referral fees

explanations.a: Wrong — this conduct violates RESPA Section 8 and may carry criminal exposure.
explanations.b: Wrong — RESPA Section 8 violations are legal violations, not merely ethical ones.
explanations.c: Wrong — the violation exists regardless of the borrower's charge; unearned fees are banned.
explanations.d: Correct — 12 USC 2607 prohibits kickbacks or things of value for referrals of settlement service business.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: When a borrower discloses financial hardship during origination, the MLO has an ethical obligation to respond thoughtfully. Steering a distressed borrower into an unsuitable product to generate compensation is unethical. An MLO's ethical responsibility when a borrower presents signs of financial stress is to:

answers.text: Recommend the highest-cost loan available to protect the lender's revenue
Proceed with origination without addressing the borrower's concerns
Present loan options honestly, discuss affordability risks, and refer the borrower to housing counseling if appropriate
Immediately decline the application without assessing all available options

explanations.a: Wrong — recommending the costliest option for revenue purposes is predatory and unethical.
explanations.b: Wrong — ignoring a distressed borrower's situation violates professional duties.
explanations.c: Correct — ethical practice requires honest presentation of options and referral to counseling when appropriate.
explanations.d: Wrong — declining without a full assessment denies the borrower due consideration.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: An MLO who is also the buyer's real estate agent in the same transaction faces competing loyalties. Dual roles create significant conflict-of-interest risk. Best practice for an MLO serving a dual MLO-and-real-estate-agent role is to:

answers.text: Never disclose the dual role, as disclosure may complicate the transaction
Fully disclose both roles in writing to all parties and obtain written acknowledgment, because the MLO owes disclosure duties to the consumer and the dual role is a material conflict
Resign from the real estate agent role immediately after contract execution
Ask the borrower to sign a blanket conflict waiver before proceeding

explanations.a: Wrong — failing to disclose material conflicts violates ethical and regulatory standards.
explanations.b: Correct — written disclosure and acknowledgment are the ethical and legally defensible approach.
explanations.c: Wrong — resigning after contract execution is too late; proactive disclosure is required.
explanations.d: Wrong — blanket conflict waivers do not eliminate the disclosure obligation.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Although most MLOs are not legal fiduciaries, ethical standards require dealing fairly with borrowers. Acting in the consumer's interest is the ethical baseline. An MLO acts most ethically when:

answers.text: Recommending loan products that fit the borrower's documented financial needs and goals, even if the MLO earns lower compensation on the best-fit product
Always recommending the highest-rate product to maximize the lender's net interest margin
Relying solely on the borrower's stated preferences without independent professional analysis
Withholding information about product options the borrower did not specifically request

explanations.a: Correct — ethical practice prioritizes the borrower's needs over compensation incentives.
explanations.b: Wrong — recommending based on rate maximization for the lender violates fair-dealing standards.
explanations.c: Wrong — pure deference without analysis abandons the MLO's professional duty.
explanations.d: Wrong — withholding material product information the borrower needs is an omission that harms the borrower.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: GLBA requires financial institutions to protect nonpublic personal information. MLOs access sensitive borrower data throughout the origination process. An MLO's legal obligation regarding consumer information under GLBA is to:

answers.text: Share consumer financial information freely with any affiliated party on request
Post borrower data publicly to demonstrate transparency to regulators
Use nonpublic personal information only for permitted purposes and safeguard it against unauthorized access
Destroy all borrower records within 30 days of closing

explanations.a: Wrong — affiliated sharing must comply with GLBA opt-out rules.
explanations.b: Wrong — public posting of consumer financial data violates GLBA.
explanations.c: Correct — GLBA's privacy and safeguards rules require limited use and protection of consumer information.
explanations.d: Wrong — record retention obligations under TILA, RESPA, and HMDA preclude prompt destruction.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: FCRA requires data furnishers to report accurate information to credit bureaus. Inaccurate reporting harms consumers' credit profiles and credit access. A creditor who furnishes consumer credit data to credit reporting agencies is obligated to:

answers.text: Report only favorable information to support consumer credit scores
Report only negative information so the bureau has complete adverse data
Withhold all consumer data until a formal dispute is filed
Provide accurate, complete, and timely information and investigate and correct inaccuracies within required timeframes

explanations.a: Wrong — one-sided reporting of favorable data would mislead the credit evaluation system.
explanations.b: Wrong — selective negative reporting also distorts the credit file.
explanations.c: Wrong — withholding data is not the remedy; accuracy and timely dispute investigation are required.
explanations.d: Correct — 15 USC 1681s-2 requires furnishers to provide accurate data and respond to disputes.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: When a financial institution suffers a breach that exposes consumer nonpublic personal information, regulatory and legal obligations arise. Timely notification allows consumers to protect themselves. Upon discovering a data breach involving consumer financial information, the institution generally must:

answers.text: Notify affected consumers and applicable regulators within the timeframes required by applicable federal and state law
Report the breach exclusively to the CFPB and take no further action
Immediately close all affected consumer accounts to prevent further harm
Notify consumers only if the breach has resulted in documented financial loss

explanations.a: Correct — federal banking guidance (e.g., the FTC Safeguards Rule) and state breach-notification laws require consumer and regulator notice.
explanations.b: Wrong — CFPB reporting alone is insufficient; consumers must also be notified.
explanations.c: Wrong — account closure may be appropriate in some cases but is not the primary legal obligation.
explanations.d: Wrong — documented loss is not a precondition for breach notification.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: The Red Flags Rule requires covered financial institutions and creditors to develop programs for detecting identity theft warning signs. Early detection protects consumers and institutions. The Red Flags Rule is designed to:

answers.text: Eliminate mortgage fraud by requiring credit freezes on all new applications
Require covered entities to identify warning signs of identity theft in their operations and take appropriate actions to prevent or mitigate it
Prevent racial discrimination in credit decisions
Mandate criminal background checks on all mortgage applicants

explanations.a: Wrong — the Red Flags Rule addresses identity theft detection, not credit freezes.
explanations.b: Correct — 16 CFR 681.1 requires a written identity theft prevention program.
explanations.c: Wrong — anti-discrimination rules are found in ECOA and the Fair Housing Act, not the Red Flags Rule.
explanations.d: Wrong — background checks are a SAFE Act licensing requirement, not a Red Flags function.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: A straw buyer scheme uses a nominee purchaser to conceal the true buyer's identity or creditworthiness. The scheme typically involves inflated prices and false representations. A straw buyer in a mortgage fraud scheme is:

answers.text: An FHA-approved borrower who uses eligible gift funds for the down payment
A borrower who purchases a second home through a family trust arrangement
A co-signer who remains liable on the note but does not occupy the property
A nominal purchaser who acts on behalf of a concealed true buyer, constituting mortgage fraud

explanations.a: Wrong — using eligible gift funds is legal; straw buyers involve concealment of the true buyer.
explanations.b: Wrong — purchasing through a trust is lawful; a straw buyer conceals the real purchaser.
explanations.c: Wrong — non-occupant co-signers are legal with disclosure; straw buyers involve fraud.
explanations.d: Correct — a straw buyer conceals the real purchaser and misrepresents material facts on a federally related loan.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Claiming owner-occupancy when the borrower intends to rent the property is a prevalent form of mortgage fraud. Owner-occupied loans typically carry more favorable terms than investor loans. Misrepresenting a borrower's occupancy intention on a mortgage application:

answers.text: Is permissible if the borrower intends to occupy within 60 days of closing
Is only a civil matter with no criminal exposure
Is mortgage fraud constituting a material misrepresentation on a federally related mortgage application
Is acceptable when the rate difference is less than 0.25 percentage points

explanations.a: Wrong — occupancy intent must be genuine at application; a 60-day window does not cure prior fraud.
explanations.b: Wrong — misrepresentation on federally related mortgages is a federal crime under 18 USC 1014.
explanations.c: Correct — intentional occupancy misrepresentation is a material misrepresentation constituting mortgage fraud.
explanations.d: Wrong — the magnitude of the rate difference does not make fraud permissible.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Inflating a borrower's income on a loan application misrepresents the ability to repay. Income fraud is one of the most common forms of application fraud. An MLO who knowingly submits an application stating income the borrower does not actually receive:

answers.text: Has committed mortgage fraud, a federal crime under 18 USC 1014
Has committed a regulatory violation but not a criminal offense
Is acting ethically if the borrower verbally confirmed the higher income figure
Is only liable if the loan subsequently defaults

explanations.a: Correct — knowingly submitting false information on a federally related mortgage application is a federal crime.
explanations.b: Wrong — submitting false statements to federally insured lenders is both a regulatory violation and a federal crime.
explanations.c: Wrong — verbal confirmation does not cure knowing submission of false income figures.
explanations.d: Wrong — criminal and civil liability arise from the fraud, not from whether the loan defaults.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: GSE and FHA guidelines require proper documentation of gift funds and prohibit using loans disguised as gifts. Representing a repayable loan as a gift understates the borrower's liabilities. Misrepresenting a repayable loan from a relative as a non-repayable gift on a mortgage application:

answers.text: Is permissible if the relative is also a co-borrower on the loan
Is a material misrepresentation on the mortgage application that constitutes mortgage fraud
Is acceptable when the loan from the relative is informal and not documented in writing
Is a minor disclosure issue that can be corrected at closing without consequence

explanations.a: Wrong — co-borrower status does not justify misclassifying a loan as a gift.
explanations.b: Correct — concealing an undisclosed liability by calling it a gift is material misrepresentation.
explanations.c: Wrong — the absence of documentation does not make the liability disappear or the misrepresentation permissible.
explanations.d: Wrong — material misrepresentation cannot be corrected without consequence.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: An air loan is a fraudulent scheme where a mortgage is originated on a property that does not exist or a transaction that has no legitimate substance. Fabricated documents support the scheme. An air loan scheme involves:

answers.text: A legitimate low-down-payment loan with no mortgage insurance requirement
Originating a loan supported only by a verbal agreement between buyer and seller
Originating a loan on a fictitious or nonexistent property using fabricated documents and false participants
Structuring loan amounts below reporting thresholds to avoid BSA scrutiny

explanations.a: Wrong — a legitimate low-down-payment loan is not a fraudulent scheme.
explanations.b: Wrong — a verbal-agreement loan may be poorly documented but is not necessarily an air loan.
explanations.c: Correct — air loans involve wholly fictitious properties and fabricated documentation.
explanations.d: Wrong — structuring below reporting thresholds is a separate BSA violation known as smurfing.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Concealing existing debts from a lender allows a borrower to present a falsely favorable financial picture. Omitted liabilities may be known to the MLO or the borrower. Failing to disclose a known debt obligation on a mortgage application:

answers.text: Is permissible when the debt was incurred before the loan application date
Is permissible when the monthly payment on the debt is below $100
Has no qualifying impact if the debt does not appear on the credit report
Is a material omission that may constitute mortgage fraud and violates the application's certification of accuracy

explanations.a: Wrong — the timing of debt incurrence does not excuse non-disclosure.
explanations.b: Wrong — no dollar threshold excuses omitting known liabilities.
explanations.c: Wrong — liability disclosure is required on the application regardless of credit-report visibility.
explanations.d: Correct — all material liabilities must be disclosed; concealing them misrepresents creditworthiness.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Predatory lending describes abusive practices that exploit vulnerable consumers through excessive fees, unsuitable products, or deceptive terms. Identifying predatory conduct is a core ethical and legal duty. Predatory lending is best characterized as:

answers.text: A pattern of abusive, unfair, or deceptive loan practices that exploit borrowers, such as loan flipping, equity stripping, or targeting vulnerable consumers with unsuitable products
Any loan with an APR above the prevailing market rate
A regulatory category defined by a specific fee threshold above conforming limits
A practice prohibited exclusively by state law with no federal enforcement

explanations.a: Correct — predatory lending encompasses patterns of abusive practices targeting borrowers, addressed by federal and state law.
explanations.b: Wrong — above-market rates alone do not define predatory lending.
explanations.c: Wrong — predatory lending is defined by conduct, not a single fee threshold.
explanations.d: Wrong — federal law (HOEPA, FTC Act, Dodd-Frank UDAAP) addresses predatory lending.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Loan flipping is a predatory practice where a lender repeatedly refinances a borrower's mortgage, generating fees without providing a genuine benefit. Each refinance may strip equity. Loan flipping typically harms the borrower by:

answers.text: Reducing the monthly payment each time through consistently lower rates
Building equity faster through shortened amortization periods
Repeatedly charging closing costs and fees that deplete the borrower's home equity without a genuine net benefit
Extending the loan term each time to lower the borrower's monthly payment

explanations.a: Wrong — flipping is harmful precisely because the borrower does not receive a net benefit.
explanations.b: Wrong — flipping typically extends amortization and increases costs, not builds equity.
explanations.c: Correct — each unnecessary refinance strips equity through fees, harming the borrower.
explanations.d: Wrong — term extension may lower payments but increases total cost; that is not a benefit.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Steering is directing a borrower toward a loan that generates more compensation for the originator when a less expensive product is available and the borrower qualifies for it. Steering violates Regulation Z. A loan originator engages in steering when:

answers.text: Recommending the loan that best fits the borrower's documented financial needs and situation
Directing a borrower to a higher-cost loan primarily to increase originator compensation when the borrower qualifies for a less expensive alternative
Presenting multiple loan options including the lowest-cost alternative for the borrower's comparison
Recommending mortgage insurance when the borrower has less than 20% down payment

explanations.a: Wrong — recommending the best-fit loan is the opposite of steering.
explanations.b: Correct — steering is directing borrowers to costlier products for originator gain under 12 CFR 1026.36(e).
explanations.c: Wrong — presenting multiple options including the best alternative satisfies the anti-steering rule.
explanations.d: Wrong — recommending required MI is disclosure, not steering.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Equity stripping depletes a property owner's equity through loans, fees, or abusive terms designed to benefit the originator or a third party. It is a hallmark of predatory lending. Equity stripping is best described as:

answers.text: The process of transferring equity through a sale-leaseback negotiated at fair market value
Refinancing at a lower interest rate to reduce the borrower's monthly costs
A home equity loan used for legitimate home improvement projects
Using loans, excessive fees, or abusive schemes to systematically deplete a homeowner's equity to the benefit of the originator or a third party

explanations.a: Wrong — a fair-market sale-leaseback is a legitimate transaction.
explanations.b: Wrong — a genuine rate-reduction refinance benefits the borrower.
explanations.c: Wrong — a home equity loan for legitimate improvement is a legal product.
explanations.d: Correct — equity stripping intentionally erodes the homeowner's equity through abusive arrangements.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Traditional redlining denied credit in minority areas. Reverse redlining targets those same communities with exploitative products rather than denying credit. Reverse redlining is:

answers.text: Targeting minority or low-income neighborhoods specifically for high-cost, abusive, or unsuitable mortgage products
The practice of refusing to make any loans in minority neighborhoods
A fair-lending best practice for low-income communities
Providing below-market-rate loans to minority borrowers as a community reinvestment benefit

explanations.a: Correct — reverse redlining victimizes the same communities historically denied credit by offering them exploitative terms.
explanations.b: Wrong — that describes traditional redlining, not reverse redlining.
explanations.c: Wrong — reverse redlining is an exploitative violation, not a best practice.
explanations.d: Wrong — below-market community lending is a CRA activity, not reverse redlining.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Predatory lenders have historically targeted older homeowners with significant home equity. Marketing abusive products to vulnerable populations is both unethical and illegal. An MLO who markets high-fee, high-rate loans exclusively to elderly homeowners with substantial home equity:

answers.text: Is engaged in a permissible niche marketing strategy
Is complying with the anti-steering rule by offering a focused product line
May be engaging in predatory targeting that implicates ECOA, the Fair Housing Act, and CFPB UDAAP authority
Is exempt from anti-discrimination rules if the product itself is legally authorized

explanations.a: Wrong — exclusive targeting of elderly homeowners for exploitative products is not permissible niche marketing.
explanations.b: Wrong — anti-steering protects consumers from higher-cost products; it does not authorize exploitative targeting.
explanations.c: Correct — age-based targeting for abusive products may violate ECOA, the Fair Housing Act, and CFPB UDAAP authority.
explanations.d: Wrong — a product's legality does not immunize discriminatory or predatory targeting practices.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Regulation N prohibits material misrepresentations in commercial communications about mortgage credit products. A statement is material if it would affect consumer decision-making. A statement is a material misrepresentation under Regulation N when:

answers.text: It is technically accurate but presented in a confusing sequence
It is a false or misleading statement about a mortgage credit product that is likely to influence the consumer's decision
It understates the APR by less than 0.125 percentage points
It omits information the consumer did not specifically inquire about

explanations.a: Wrong — confusing presentation may be an issue but is distinct from a false statement.
explanations.b: Correct — 12 CFR 1014 prohibits false, deceptive, or misleading statements likely to affect consumer decisions.
explanations.c: Wrong — minor APR understatements that fall within TILA's tolerances are not Reg N material misrepresentations.
explanations.d: Wrong — material omissions are a related but separate concern; this question addresses affirmative false statements.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: An omission of a material fact can be as harmful as an affirmative misrepresentation. Consumers rely on complete information to make informed decisions. An MLO who fails to disclose that the loan carries a prepayment penalty:

answers.text: Has acted ethically if the penalty amount is less than 1% of the loan balance
Is exempt if the consumer did not specifically ask about prepayment terms
Must disclose only if the applicable state law independently requires it
Has omitted a material term that must be disclosed under Regulation Z

explanations.a: Wrong — the penalty amount does not determine the disclosure obligation.
explanations.b: Wrong — TILA disclosure requirements apply regardless of whether the consumer asks.
explanations.c: Wrong — Regulation Z requires prepayment penalty disclosure regardless of state law.
explanations.d: Correct — 12 CFR 1026.37(b)(5) and 1026.38 require prepayment penalty disclosure on the LE and CD.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Regulation N prohibits material misrepresentations in mortgage advertising. The rule covers commercial communications broadly. Regulation N is violated when an advertisement:

answers.text: States the true APR and the monthly payment together in a clear format
Includes the required NMLS unique identifier and the lender's legal name
Claims a guaranteed interest rate without disclosing that the rate is only available to certain qualified borrowers
Prominently discloses all terms and conditions required by Regulation Z

explanations.a: Wrong — accurate APR and payment disclosure is lawful.
explanations.b: Wrong — including NMLS ID and lender name is required, not a violation.
explanations.c: Correct — claiming a guaranteed rate without accurate qualification disclosures is a material misrepresentation under Reg N.
explanations.d: Wrong — full Regulation Z disclosure is required and compliant.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: The law treats intentional misrepresentations more severely than negligent ones. Intent affects both criminal exposure and civil liability. A knowing misrepresentation on a mortgage application differs from a negligent one in that:

answers.text: A knowing misrepresentation involves intentional falsehood and may constitute criminal mortgage fraud under 18 USC 1014, while negligent misrepresentation involves careless mistake and typically triggers civil liability
Both are treated identically under federal mortgage fraud statutes
Only knowing misrepresentations carry any legal consequences
Negligent misrepresentations are more serious because they affect more consumers

explanations.a: Correct — 18 USC 1014 criminalizes knowing false statements; negligent errors are addressed through civil remedies.
explanations.b: Wrong — knowing and negligent misrepresentations carry different consequences.
explanations.c: Wrong — negligent misrepresentations may trigger RESPA, TILA, or state-law civil liability.
explanations.d: Wrong — knowing criminal fraud is more serious than careless mistake in legal treatment.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Altering a Closing Disclosure or HUD-1 falsifies a federally required document. Document falsification is a form of mortgage fraud. An MLO who alters figures on a Closing Disclosure to conceal fees that were not disclosed on the Loan Estimate:

answers.text: Has committed a TRID disclosure violation only, with no criminal exposure
Has falsified a federally required document and may face criminal liability for mortgage fraud under federal law
Is acting within their authority to correct clerical errors on disclosure forms
Is required to do so when the borrower requests a revised closing figure

explanations.a: Wrong — falsifying required documents carries criminal exposure beyond a TRID violation.
explanations.b: Correct — deliberately altering a federally required disclosure constitutes document fraud.
explanations.c: Wrong — correcting genuine clerical errors is permissible; concealing undisclosed fees is fraud.
explanations.d: Wrong — borrower requests do not authorize fraud.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Appraisal fraud often involves an appraiser or MLO conspiring to report a falsely inflated property value to support a larger loan. The inflated value misrepresents the lender's collateral. Obtaining or submitting an appraisal with a falsely inflated value:

answers.text: Is permissible if an independent lender review confirms the inflated figure
Is only a concern when the property is non-owner-occupied investment real estate
Is acceptable if the sales price independently supports the inflated value
Constitutes appraisal fraud and is a false statement to a federally insured or regulated lender under 18 USC 1014

explanations.a: Wrong — lender review does not cure an intentionally inflated appraisal.
explanations.b: Wrong — appraisal fraud on any property type is a federal crime.
explanations.c: Wrong — a sales price can itself be part of the fraud; independence of value is required.
explanations.d: Correct — submitting a knowingly inflated appraisal is a material false statement under federal fraud statutes.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Regulation Z prohibits persons with an interest in the transaction from coercing or improperly influencing an appraiser. Pressure to reach a predetermined value is a specific fraud form. A lender who contacts an appraiser and threatens to stop using them unless the appraiser raises their value conclusion:

answers.text: Has violated 12 CFR 1026.42(c) by coercing the appraiser and may have committed appraisal fraud
Has acted within their right to seek a second appraisal opinion
Has properly exercised their right to request a reconsideration of value
Is permitted to encourage the appraiser to consider comparable sales that may have been missed

explanations.a: Correct — threatening an appraiser to obtain a higher value violates the appraisal independence rule and constitutes fraud.
explanations.b: Wrong — ordering a second appraisal is legal; threatening the appraiser to change a value is not.
explanations.c: Wrong — a legitimate reconsideration of value provides missing data; threatening to remove the appraiser is coercion.
explanations.d: Wrong — suggesting missed comparables is permissible; threatening the appraiser to raise value is coercion.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: A fraudulent sale-leaseback targets distressed homeowners who face foreclosure. The scheme strips equity under the pretense of a rescue. A fraudulent sale-leaseback scheme typically involves:

answers.text: A legitimate investor purchasing a distressed property at fair market value with full transparency
A bankruptcy estate selling property and renting it back for a temporary period
Exploiting a distressed homeowner by purchasing their property at below-market value under the guise of rescue, leaving the former owner as a tenant at risk of eviction
A conventional home sale with a post-closing rental agreement disclosed to the lender

explanations.a: Wrong — a legitimate fair-market purchase with transparency is not fraudulent.
explanations.b: Wrong — a bankruptcy estate sale is a court-supervised process, not a fraudulent scheme.
explanations.c: Correct — the fraud lies in deceiving a vulnerable homeowner and stripping their equity through deceptive below-market purchase.
explanations.d: Wrong — a disclosed post-closing lease is a legitimate transaction.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: An appraiser who selects only above-market comparable sales to reach a predetermined value is manipulating the appraisal. Selective comparable use distorts the market-value opinion. An appraiser who deliberately excludes lower-value comparable sales to inflate the reported value:

answers.text: Is exercising permissible professional judgment within USPAP standards
Has committed appraisal fraud by manipulating value through biased comparable selection
Is applying the highest and best use analysis correctly
Is required to do so when the borrower's purchase price exceeds market value

explanations.a: Wrong — USPAP requires objective, unbiased selection of comparables.
explanations.b: Correct — intentional exclusion of unfavorable comparables to reach a predetermined value constitutes appraisal fraud.
explanations.c: Wrong — highest and best use is a separate analysis; it does not justify biased comparable selection.
explanations.d: Wrong — no obligation requires an appraiser to match or support the purchase price.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Fraudulent property flipping uses sham transactions, inflated appraisals, and coordinated participants to rapidly inflate a property's recorded value. The scheme enables oversized loans and generates large profits for conspirators. Fraudulent property flipping typically involves:

answers.text: Legal arm's-length property purchases and sales at current market prices
Normal investor renovations that increase property value before resale
A property placed in a trust to facilitate a longer-term tax-deferred exchange

Collusion between sellers, buyers, appraisers, and sometimes MLOs using sham transactions and fabricated appraisals to artificially inflate recorded sales prices and generate fraudulently large loan amounts

explanations.a: Wrong — arm's-length transactions at market prices are lawful flipping.
explanations.b: Wrong — legitimate renovation and resale at a higher price is legal.
explanations.c: Wrong — 1031 exchanges are legal tax strategies, not fraud.
explanations.d: Correct — fraudulent flipping involves coordinated misrepresentation to inflate value and extract loan proceeds.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: True-name identity theft uses a real person's actual identifying information to obtain credit without that person's knowledge. Mortgage applications may reveal red flags. True-name identity theft in a mortgage application involves:

answers.text: Using a real person's name, SSN, and other identifying information without that person's knowledge or consent to obtain a mortgage loan
A borrower accidentally misspelling their name on the application
An MLO completing the application on the borrower's behalf with full authorization
A borrower providing a nickname in place of their legal name on the form

explanations.a: Correct — true-name identity theft involves using a real person's identity without consent for fraudulent gain.
explanations.b: Wrong — an innocent spelling error is a clerical issue, not identity theft.
explanations.c: Wrong — completing the application with authorization is lawful assistance, not fraud.
explanations.d: Wrong — a nickname discrepancy may warrant verification but is not identity theft.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Synthetic identity fraud combines real and fabricated personal information to create a fictitious person. It is difficult to detect because no single victim's credit file is fully compromised. A synthetic identity in mortgage fraud typically involves:

answers.text: Forging a deceased person's complete official identity documents
Stealing one real person's complete identity including SSN and name
Combining a real Social Security number with fabricated personal details such as a different name, date of birth, or address to create a fraudulent identity
Using a child's SSN with the child's knowledge to build a credit profile

explanations.a: Wrong — using a deceased person's documents is a form of true-name fraud, not synthetic.
explanations.b: Wrong — stealing a complete identity is true-name theft.
explanations.c: Correct — synthetic identity fraud creates a new artificial person by mixing real SSN data with fabricated details.
explanations.d: Wrong — using a child's SSN even with informal consent constitutes fraud.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: MLOs and creditors must have programs to detect warning signs of identity theft. Early detection protects consumers. A common red flag suggesting possible identity theft on a mortgage application is:

answers.text: A consumer who provides professional references from the same employer
Inconsistencies between the application, credit report, and identity documents, such as different address, name variation, or Social Security number mismatch
A consumer who applies for the mortgage online rather than in person
A consumer who has more than one open credit card account

explanations.a: Wrong — professional references from the same employer are not a red flag.
explanations.b: Correct — document inconsistencies are a primary identity-theft red flag under the Red Flags Rule.
explanations.c: Wrong — online applications are not inherently suspicious.
explanations.d: Wrong — multiple credit cards are common and not a red flag.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: The Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination in the sale, rental, and financing of housing. Protected classes are defined in the statute. The Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination based on:

answers.text: Credit score, loan-to-value ratio, and debt-to-income ratio
State of residence, employment type, and income source
Property location, appraised value, and property condition
Race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, and disability

explanations.a: Wrong — credit score and financial ratios are underwriting factors, not protected classes.
explanations.b: Wrong — these are not FHA protected classes.
explanations.c: Wrong — property characteristics are not FHA protected classes.
explanations.d: Correct — 42 USC 3604-3605 list these seven protected classes.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Disparate treatment is a form of intentional or de facto discrimination where similarly situated applicants are treated differently. It is a recognized form of fair-lending violation. Disparate treatment in mortgage lending occurs when:

answers.text: A lender applies the same rate to all borrowers regardless of credit profile
A lender applies the same qualifying ratios to all loan applicants
A lender applies different qualifying standards, products, or pricing to similarly qualified applicants based on a protected class characteristic
A lender denies a loan to a borrower who fails to meet credit standards

explanations.a: Wrong — uniform treatment across borrowers does not constitute disparate treatment.
explanations.b: Wrong — consistent application of the same ratios supports non-discrimination.
explanations.c: Correct — treating similarly qualified borrowers differently on the basis of protected class is disparate treatment.
explanations.d: Wrong — denying loans based on legitimate credit criteria is lawful.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Disparate impact occurs when a facially neutral policy disproportionately harms a protected class. Neither intentional discrimination nor knowledge of the disparity is required. A disparate impact claim in mortgage lending requires:

answers.text: Showing that a facially neutral policy or practice has a statistically significant adverse effect on a protected class, even without discriminatory intent
Evidence that the lender explicitly stated a discriminatory purpose
Proof of intentional discrimination in every individual transaction affected
A criminal conviction of an MLO under the Fair Housing Act

explanations.a: Correct — disparate impact under ECOA and the Fair Housing Act can be proven through statistical evidence of disproportionate harm without discriminatory intent.
explanations.b: Wrong — disparate impact does not require explicit discriminatory statements.
explanations.c: Wrong — disparate impact is a pattern-based theory, not a transaction-by-transaction intent analysis.
explanations.d: Wrong — criminal conviction is not required to establish disparate impact.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Redlining is the practice of systematically denying credit or limiting services in geographic areas based on the racial or ethnic makeup of those neighborhoods. Redlining violates both ECOA and the Fair Housing Act. Redlining is best described as:

answers.text: Pricing loans higher in high-cost metropolitan areas based on operating costs
The illegal practice of refusing to lend or making credit unavailable to residents in minority or low-income neighborhoods based on the racial or ethnic composition of those areas
A geographic pricing strategy based on actuarially justified default rate differences
A fair-lending tool used by regulators to identify underserved communities

explanations.a: Wrong — geographic cost-of-business pricing is distinct from redlining.
explanations.b: Correct — redlining is the illegal geographic exclusion of minority communities from credit.
explanations.c: Wrong — default rate differences do not justify race-based geographic lending exclusions.
explanations.d: Wrong — regulators identify redlining to prosecute it, not to endorse it.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Pricing discrimination involves charging members of a protected class higher rates or fees than similarly qualified borrowers outside that class. Statistical patterns can constitute evidence. An MLO who consistently quotes higher rates to minority borrowers with comparable credit profiles:

answers.text: Is complying with risk-based pricing rules if credit scores are within the same range
Is acting lawfully as long as the rates remain below HOEPA's high-cost thresholds
Is exercising appropriate discretion in exercising a floating rate policy
May be engaging in pricing discrimination in violation of ECOA and the Fair Housing Act

explanations.a: Wrong — risk-based pricing based on credit score does not justify pricing by race.
explanations.b: Wrong — HOEPA thresholds limit high-cost loans; they do not authorize discriminatory pricing.
explanations.c: Wrong — subjective pricing discretion that produces racial disparities can constitute discrimination.
explanations.d: Correct — disparate pricing based on race violates ECOA and the Fair Housing Act.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: ECOA prohibits credit discrimination on specified bases. The list includes civil rights protections and credit-specific additions. ECOA's prohibited bases for discrimination include:

answers.text: Credit score, loan-to-value, and loan-to-income ratio
Property location, appraised value, and years of employment
Race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, receipt of public assistance, and exercise of rights under the CCPA
Employment status, debt type, and income stability

explanations.a: Wrong — these are underwriting criteria, not ECOA protected bases.
explanations.b: Wrong — these are property and employment factors, not ECOA protected bases.
explanations.c: Correct — 15 USC 1691 and 12 CFR 1002.4 list these as prohibited bases.
explanations.d: Wrong — these are also underwriting criteria, not ECOA protected classes.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Proxy discrimination uses a facially neutral factor that correlates with a protected class as a substitute for that class in decision-making. It is a sophisticated disparate treatment theory. An example of potential proxy discrimination is:

answers.text: A lender who applies stricter underwriting to applicants from specific ZIP codes that closely correlate with minority population concentration
A lender who applies the same credit score minimum to all applicants
A lender who applies the same maximum debt-to-income ratio to every borrower
A lender who requires two years of employment history from all borrowers uniformly

explanations.a: Correct — using ZIP codes as a substitute for race when they are closely correlated constitutes proxy discrimination.
explanations.b: Wrong — applying a uniform credit score minimum is facially neutral and consistently applied.
explanations.c: Wrong — a uniform DTI limit applied to all is not discriminatory on its face.
explanations.d: Wrong — a uniform employment history requirement applied to all is not discriminatory.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: The Fair Housing Act's familial status protected class prevents discrimination against families with children and certain other household types. The definition is broader than just nuclear families. Under the Fair Housing Act, familial status protection covers:

answers.text: Only legally married couples with biological children under the age of 18
Households that include one or more children under age 18, pregnant persons, and persons in the process of obtaining legal custody of a child
Only same-sex couples with adopted children who are under the age of 18
All households that include any person who is 65 years of age or older

explanations.a: Wrong — familial status protection is not limited to married couples or biological children.
explanations.b: Correct — 42 USC 3602(k) defines familial status to include these categories.
explanations.c: Wrong — familial status is not limited by the parents' relationship or the means of custody.
explanations.d: Wrong — age 65+ households are not the definition of familial status.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Structuring involves deliberately breaking up transactions to avoid BSA reporting requirements. It is a federal crime regardless of whether the underlying funds are from illegal activity. Structuring is:

answers.text: Permissible when the borrower is conducting legitimate business transactions
Allowed when the cumulative transactions total less than $50,000
Only illegal if the broken-up cash derives from criminal proceeds
Illegal under the Bank Secrecy Act regardless of the source of funds, because the purpose is to evade filing requirements

explanations.a: Wrong — structuring is illegal regardless of the source or legitimacy of the funds.
explanations.b: Wrong — there is no $50,000 aggregate exemption.
explanations.c: Wrong — structuring is illegal based on the intent to evade reporting, irrespective of the fund source.
explanations.d: Correct — 31 USC 5324 prohibits structuring to evade reporting requirements regardless of fund origin.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Financial institutions must file a Currency Transaction Report for cash transactions above a specified dollar threshold. The filing is automatic and based solely on the amount. A Currency Transaction Report must be filed when a cash transaction involves more than:

answers.text: 5,000 dollars in currency
25,000 dollars in currency
10,000 dollars in currency
50,000 dollars in currency

explanations.a: Wrong — 5,000 dollars is the SAR monetary threshold, not the CTR threshold.
explanations.b: Wrong — 25,000 dollars is not the CTR threshold.
explanations.c: Correct — 31 USC 5313 and 31 CFR 1010.311 require a CTR for cash transactions exceeding $10,000.
explanations.d: Wrong — 50,000 dollars exceeds the CTR trigger threshold.

questions.name: Ethics
questions.text: Filing a SAR is required for suspicious transactions above the threshold. The MLO has both a legal and ethical duty to report suspected fraud or money laundering. An MLO who suspects a borrower is engaged in mortgage fraud must:

answers.text: Report the suspicion through the compliance department and support filing a SAR if required, without tipping off the borrower to the report
Confront the borrower directly and ask them to explain the suspicious activity before filing
Continue the transaction while planning to inform the regulator at consummation
Disclose the SAR filing to the borrower and seek their consent before submitting it

explanations.a: Correct — BSA requires SAR filing and prohibits tipping off the subject under 31 CFR 1020.320.
explanations.b: Wrong — direct confrontation constitutes prohibited tipping off.
explanations.c: Wrong — continuing the transaction while planning future notification is improper.
explanations.d: Wrong — disclosing a SAR to its subject violates the anti-tipping provision.
